weekLabel: Week 14 · Meeting A · Classification, Confusion Matrices, and Model Cards

slides.title: A model that's usually right can still be dangerously wrong for the cases that matter.
slides.subtitle: Classification as a decision rule — confusion matrix, precision vs. recall, choosing a threshold from consequences, cross_val_score, and the model card
slides.teaching: Open by naming today's fork: Week 13 asked 'how far off is the number?' (regression). Today asks a different question: 'go or no-go?' Same 140-row Radley Hall portfolio, same fitted-model idea, but the target is now a decision, not a quantity. Preview that Meeting B splits into two tracks — go/no-go classification (Track A) or continued regression refinement (Track B) — but today's theory applies to both.

slides.title: A threshold decision needs a reason, not a default
slides.statement: Every classifier's 0/1 answer hides a choice — a threshold on a predicted probability — and picking that threshold is a judgment about which mistake costs more.
slides.supporting: Today's central case: for Radley Hall's go/no-go call, a false 'go' (approving a design that actually fails code) is far more dangerous than a false 'no-go' (discarding a design that would have passed). That asymmetry, not the default 0.5 cutoff, is what should set the threshold.
slides.teaching: This is the plan's explicit ask: teach the REASONING behind a threshold choice, not just the arithmetic. Return to this exact sentence after the threshold-sweep table later in the deck.

outcomes.head: Read
outcomes.body: Read a confusion matrix (TN/FP/FN/TP) and state, in plain language, what each of the four cells means for a real go/no-go design decision.

outcomes.head: Compute
outcomes.body: Hand-compute precision, recall, and F1 from raw confusion-matrix counts, and explain what each metric answers that the others don't.

outcomes.head: Choose
outcomes.body: Choose an operating threshold from a threshold-sweep table by reasoning about which error (false positive or false negative) is more dangerous — not by defaulting to 0.5.

outcomes.head: Explain
outcomes.body: Explain what cross_val_score adds beyond a single train/test split, and what a model card must state about a model's scope and limits.

slides.teaching: All four map directly onto Meeting B's Track A studio deliverable (confusion matrix + model card) and onto Project 2 Part IV's go/no-go integration.

items: From a number to a decision: classification as a decision rule
The confusion matrix: four ways a go/no-go call can land
Precision, recall, and choosing a threshold from real consequences
cross_val_score and the model card: does it hold up, and what does it promise
slides.teaching: Tell students Track A and Track B split next class, but everything today applies to both — Track B's model card and cross-validated R² range use the exact same vocabulary as Track A's confusion matrix and threshold.

slides.title: Same portfolio, a different question

left.head: Week 13 asked
left.body: How far off is the predicted eui_kwh_m2yr from the actual number? Regression fits a continuous target, and MAE/RMSE/R² measure how close the guesses land.

right.head: Week 14 asks
right.body: Does this design meet code, yes or no? meets_code = 1 if eui_kwh_m2yr <= 27.0, else 0 — the exact same 140-row Radley Hall portfolio and design variables, only the target and the model type change.

slides.teaching: Emphasize this is not a new dataset: same wwr/shade_m/glazing_shgc/compactness columns as Week 13, only the target and the model type change.

slides.title: Classification, defined
slides.definition: A classification model predicts which CATEGORY a row belongs to, instead of a continuous number. Here, just two categories: meets_code=1 ('go') or meets_code=0 ('no-go') — the same 140-row portfolio Week 13 used, only the target and model type change.

example.head: Under the hood: probability, then threshold
example.body: A classifier like LogisticRegression first predicts a PROBABILITY between 0 and 1 (predict_proba), then a threshold turns that probability into the final yes/no decision. The decision rule, not just the model, is what you are building today.

slides.note: Not the same as a category-valued FEATURE like orientation (N/E/S/W) — that's an input column. Classification predicts the category OUTPUT (meets_code), not a category input.
slides.teaching: Stress the two-step structure — probability, then threshold — early; every later slide (confusion matrix, threshold sweep) depends on students holding onto this distinction.

slides.title: The label: meets_code, and how balanced it is
rows: 84 train / 28 validation / 28 untouched final test; both splits stratified
slides.callout: Stratification preserves the class proportion across train, validation, and final-test roles. Train fits coefficients; validation selects the threshold; final test is opened once after the policy is frozen.
slides.teaching: Point out stratify=y keeps roughly the same 92/48 proportion in both the train and test slices — worth naming as a keyword argument students haven't seen before, one line, no deep dive.

slides.title: From design variables to a go/no-go call

steps.label: TRAIN
steps.head: Fit on 84 rows
steps.body: The model learns coefficients from the training partition only.

steps.label: VALIDATE
steps.head: Choose the policy on 28 rows
steps.body: Sweep thresholds and apply a predeclared consequence rule.

steps.label: FREEZE
steps.head: Lock model + threshold
steps.body: Freeze both before seeing any final-test outcomes.

steps.label: TEST
steps.head: Open 28 rows once
steps.body: Report final confusion counts and metrics without retuning.

slides.teaching: Have students name what may be decided at each stage. The final test measures the frozen pipeline; it is not another tuning set.

slides.title: Reserve train, validation, and final test
slides.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

FEATURES = ['wwr','shade_m','glazing_shgc','compactness']
X, y = df[FEATURES], df['meets_code']
X_dev, X_test, y_dev, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=42, stratify=y)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_dev, y_dev, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y_dev)
slides.explainHead: Split before fitting or choosing a threshold
slides.explainBody: The two deterministic stratified splits create 84 training, 28 validation, and 28 untouched final-test rows. Only validation may guide the operating threshold.
slides.teaching: Ask students to name the role of each partition before fitting the classifier.

slides.title: Fit on training rows; inspect coefficients
slides.code:
clf = LogisticRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
print('rows:', len(X_train), len(X_val), len(X_test))
print('coef_:', clf.coef_.round(4))
slides.explainBody: Train learns coefficients; validation chooses the threshold policy; final test stays sealed. Coefficient directions are fitted associations, not causal effects.
slides.teaching: Point to 84/28/28 and ask which partition may influence the threshold: validation only.

slides.title: Confusion matrix, defined
slides.definition: A 2×2 table that cross-tabulates predicted classes against actual outcomes. Every evaluated design lands in one cell after a threshold is applied. During selection we read a validation matrix; final reporting uses a separate untouched test matrix.

example.head: The four cells, named
example.body: TN and TP are correct calls; FP and FN are different errors with different consequences. Always label which partition and threshold produced the matrix.

slides.note: A confusion matrix is built from PREDICTED class labels (0/1), not the raw probability — it already assumes a threshold has been applied (default 0.5 unless stated otherwise).
slides.teaching: Set up the anatomy and predict slides that follow: students should be able to name all four cells before seeing a single real number.

slides.title: Anatomy: the validation confusion_matrix() call

parts.label: The function
parts.body: From sklearn.metrics — compares actual vs. predicted, returns the table.

parts.label: Actual validation labels
parts.body: The 28 validation outcomes used to choose the operating policy.

slides.teaching: Name this as validation evidence. The untouched final test is still sealed and appears only after the threshold is frozen.

slides.title: Predict: how many truly-compliant designs get caught?
slides.code:
val_pred = clf.predict(X_val)  # candidate threshold 0.5
tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_val, val_pred).ravel()
print('TP =', tp)
slides.question: How many of 9 compliant validation designs are caught (TP)?
slides.why: TP=6. The model misses 3 of 9 compliant validation designs, so recall=6/9=0.667.
slides.teaching: Call this a validation result every time. The final test is still sealed.

slides.title: Validation confusion matrix at threshold 0.5
slides.callout: 28 validation designs. This matrix may guide the threshold choice; it is not the final reported performance.
slides.teaching: This confirms the predict slide's TP=6 answer. Read the validation table aloud: 18 true negatives, 6 true positives, 1 false positive, and 3 false negatives. The final test remains sealed.

slides.title: Four validation outcomes, one consequence each

left.head: True negative / true positive
left.body: TN (18): model says no-go and the design fails code — correctly discarded. TP (6): model says go and the design meets code — correctly approved.

right.head: False positive / false negative
right.body: FP (1): model says GO but the design fails code — a dangerous review failure. FN (3): model says no-go on a design that would pass — a viable option discarded.

slides.teaching: Point to the validation matrix while naming each cell and consequence. These counts support threshold selection; they are not final-test performance.

slides.title: Precision, defined
slides.definition: Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of every validation design called 'go,' what fraction actually meets code? At 0.5: 6 / (6 + 1) = 0.857.

example.head: The question it answers
example.body: 'When this model says GO, how often can I trust it?' High precision means few false 'go' calls — exactly the property that matters most given the false-positive-is-dangerous argument coming up.

slides.teaching: Say the plain-English question out loud every time a metric is introduced — students retain 'when it says X, can I trust it' far better than the raw formula alone.

slides.title: Recall, defined
slides.definition: Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of every validation design that actually meets code, what fraction did the model catch? At 0.5: 6 / (6 + 3) = 0.667.

example.head: The question it answers
example.body: At validation threshold 0.5, recall=0.667: the model catches 6 of 9 truly compliant validation designs and misses 3.

slides.teaching: Translate 0.667 back into 6 caught and 3 missed; the count makes the consequence legible.

slides.title: Precision and recall move in opposite directions

left.head: Raise the threshold
left.body: Precision tends to rise — fewer, more-confident 'go' calls, since only the highest-probability designs clear a higher bar. Recall falls — more truly good designs get missed, since some clear 0.5 but not the higher cutoff.

right.head: Lower the threshold
right.body: Recall tends to rise — more truly good designs get caught. Precision falls — more of the designs the model calls 'go' turn out not to actually meet code. You cannot raise both at once with the same fitted model.

slides.teaching: This is the pivot into F1 (next slide) and the threshold-sweep table — make sure students can state the trade-off in their own words before either appears.

slides.title: F1, defined
slides.definition: F1 = 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall). At validation threshold 0.5: F1 = 0.750.

example.head: What it hides
example.body: F1 balances the two metrics but does not say WHICH error (false positive or false negative) is being made — that is why today's threshold decision uses the full sweep table, not F1 alone.

slides.note: F1 does not encode the consequence rule. Select a threshold with a stated operational requirement, then evaluate the frozen choice on the untouched final test.
slides.teaching: F1 summarizes a balance but does not encode the FPR≤10% operational rule. Keep metric and policy reasoning separate.

slides.title: Precision and recall, across five thresholds
slides.chartTitle: Validation precision and recall vs. threshold
slides.explainHead: The selection rule picks 0.5—not because it is the default
slides.explainBody: Require validation false-positive rate ≤10%, then maximize recall. Threshold 0.4 narrowly fails (2/19=10.5%); 0.5 qualifies (1/19=5.3%) and retains 6/9 positives. Threshold 0.6 gives up too much recall.
slides.teaching: Point out that 0.4 has attractive recall but narrowly fails the declared FPR limit; 0.5 is the qualifying threshold with the highest recall.

slides.title: Hand-computing precision, recall, and F1 from raw counts
slides.code:
TN, FP, FN, TP = 18, 1, 3, 6
precision = TP / (TP + FP)
recall = TP / (TP + FN)
f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
print(round(precision, 4), round(recall, 4), round(f1, 4))
slides.explainHead: No sklearn call needed — just the four counts
slides.explainBody: These validation counts reproduce sklearn's metrics. The final-test matrix remains sealed until selection is complete.
slides.teaching: Students redo the arithmetic from 18/1/3/6 before using metric functions.

slides.title: One function for every threshold, not one at a time
slides.code:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

def threshold_sweep(y_true, probs, cuts: list) -> None:
    """Print confusion counts and guarded rates."""
    for t in cuts:
        pred = (probs >= t).astype(int)
        tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(
            y_true, pred).ravel()
        precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
        recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
        print(t, "TN FP FN TP:", tn, fp, fn, tp,
              "| P", round(precision, 3),
              "R", round(recall, 3))
slides.explainHead: The previous slide's arithmetic, now guarded and looped
slides.explainBody: The formulas are unchanged when denominators are positive. The inline guards return 0.0 when a threshold predicts no positives, so the full candidate grid can be printed without a division error.
slides.teaching: Use 0.3–0.7 as a candidate grid, not a recommendation. The predeclared FPR/recall rule on the next slide selects 0.5; the guard only makes the 0.7 edge case explicit.

slides.title: ...continued: five cutoffs, one printed sweep
slides.code:
probs_val = clf.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
cuts = [0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7]
threshold_sweep(y_val, probs_val, cuts)
chosen = 0.5  # predeclared FPR/recall rule
print('frozen threshold:', chosen)
slides.explainHead: A consequence rule turns a sweep into a reproducible choice
slides.explainBody: Before opening the final test, require validation FPR≤10%, then maximize recall among qualifying thresholds. The selected value is 0.5 by rule, not by default.
slides.teaching: Verify all five validation rows, apply the predeclared FPR rule, freeze 0.5, and only then proceed to final testing.

slides.title: Threshold, defined
slides.definition: The probability cutoff — default 0.5 — above which predict_proba's output becomes a 'go' call. Everything below the cutoff becomes 'no-go.' Nothing forces you to keep the default.

example.head: Same model, different cutoffs
example.body: Raising the threshold from 0.5 to 0.6 does not refit anything — it only changes which predicted probabilities cross the line into a 'go' call. The next slides sweep five different cutoffs on this exact model.

slides.note: Changing the threshold changes ZERO coefficients — clf.coef_ and clf.intercept_ stay identical. Only the FINAL yes/no decision, and therefore the confusion matrix, changes.
slides.teaching: This is the term the rest of the deck's threshold-sweep table and consequences argument both depend on — do not let 'threshold' and 'coefficient' blur together here.

slides.title: Predict: F1 at the strictest threshold
slides.code:
for t in [0.5, 0.6, 0.7]:
    pred_t = (probs_val >= t).astype(int)
    print(t, precision_score(y_val, pred_t, zero_division=0),
          recall_score(y_val, pred_t, zero_division=0))
slides.question: At threshold 0.7, TP=0. What is the F1 score?
options: 1.000 — perfect, since there are no false positives
0.000 — precision and recall both collapse to zero
slides.why: TP=0 collapses both precision and recall to 0.000 by convention — calling nothing 'go' earns no credit.
slides.teaching: Let students commit to a letter first — many pick 1.000, reasoning 'zero false positives' without checking that zero true positives also means zero credit.

slides.title: Threshold sweep: same model, only the cutoff changes
slides.callout: Same fitted model and 28 validation designs; only the cutoff changes. Use these rows to select the policy—never to report final performance.
slides.teaching: Walk the table left to right: as threshold rises, FP falls toward 0 and precision rises toward 1.0, while FN rises and recall collapses toward 0. At 0.7, precision and recall both hit 0.000 — confirming the predict slide's answer.

slides.title: Which mistake is more dangerous here?
slides.statement: A false positive—saying GO when a design actually fails code—creates a costly failed review. A false negative discards a viable option.
slides.supporting: Turn that asymmetry into a reproducible validation rule: require FPR≤10%, then maximize recall among qualifying thresholds. Threshold 0.4 narrowly fails; 0.5 qualifies and retains far more positives than 0.6. The value equals the software default only by coincidence.
slides.teaching: Ask students to defend the rule before showing which threshold wins. Selection must use validation data, not the final test.

slides.title: Freeze the operating point: threshold = 0.5
rows: FPR ≤10%; among qualifying thresholds, maximize recall
FPR improves to 0%, but recall collapses to 0.111
slides.callout: Now freeze the model and threshold. The final test may be opened once; its result cannot send us back to retune.
slides.teaching: Say explicitly: the chosen value happens to equal the default, but the reasoning is not 'because 0.5 is the default.'

slides.title: cross_val_score, defined
slides.definition: Refits the model across several development-data folds and returns one score per held-out fold. Here it checks default-0.5 accuracy variability on the 112-row development set; it does not select or validate the threshold policy and it does not touch the final test.

example.head: The question it answers
example.body: 'Does this hold up on data it hasn't seen?' Five folds means five honest re-tries, not five chances to cherry-pick the best-looking one.

slides.note: Fold-to-fold scores describe variability across these partitions. They are not a confidence interval, a prediction interval, or proof that a policy generalizes.
slides.teaching: Name the core question explicitly: 'does this hold up on data it hasn't seen' — that phrase is the entire point of this slide.

slides.title: cross_val_score in action — does this hold up?
slides.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(), X_dev, y_dev,
                         cv=cv, scoring='accuracy')
print(scores.round(4), round(scores.mean(), 4))
slides.explainBody: Accuracy varies from 0.6364 to 0.8636 across folds. This checks a default-threshold scoring pipeline, not the consequence-selected threshold, and it is not an interval for a new case.
slides.teaching: Label this as development-only default-threshold accuracy variability. It neither selects the threshold nor produces a confidence interval.

slides.title: Freeze, then open the final test once
rows: choose 0.5 under FPR≤10%, then max-recall rule
slides.callout: The final-test drop is the honest result. Do not retune after seeing it; revise only in a future, separately evaluated model version.
slides.teaching: Read the performance drop without softening it. Once the final test is opened, its result is reported—not used to retune.

slides.title: Model card, defined
slides.definition: A one-page, plain-language statement of what a fitted model was trained on, what it's for, and — just as important — what it should NOT be trusted to do. It ships WITH the model, not buried in code comments.

example.head: Why it's today's deliverable
example.body: A confusion matrix and a threshold are only useful to someone who also knows the model's training range, its stated operating threshold, and its honest, cross-validated accuracy — not just its single best-looking number.

slides.teaching: Frame the model card as the professional artifact of this session: everything before this slide becomes an entry on this one page.

slides.title: Radley Hall go/no-go classifier — model card
rows: 84 train / 28 validation / 28 untouched final test from n=140 synthetic variants
0.5; selected on validation by FPR≤10%, then maximize recall
TN=16, FP=2, FN=8, TP=2; precision=0.500, recall=0.200, F1=0.286
synthetic data; no causal claim; do not extrapolate beyond stated feature ranges
slides.teaching: This is a real, filled-in model card, not a blank template — walk it row by row and ask students what would change if THEIR Project 2 dataset and threshold were substituted in.

slides.title: Read a new confusion matrix
slides.prompt: A second design portfolio's classifier reports TN=15, FP=2, FN=4, TP=9 on its test set. Compute precision, recall, and F1 by hand — then say, in one sentence, what kind of mistake this model makes more often.
steps: Compute precision = TP/(TP+FP) and recall = TP/(TP+FN).
Compute F1 from those two values.
Decide: does this model lean toward false positives or false negatives, and how do you know from the numbers alone?
State which error would worry you more if this were a real go/no-go call, and why.
slides.teaching: Correct answers: precision=9/11=0.818, recall=9/13=0.692, F1=2(0.818)(0.692)/(0.818+0.692)=0.750. FN=4 is larger than FP=2, so this model actually leans toward MISSING compliant designs (false negatives) — the opposite pattern from today's Radley Hall model at threshold 0.5, a deliberate contrast, not a repeat.

slides.title: Choose a threshold from consequences, not a default
slides.prompt: A structural-screening classifier flags whether a connection detail needs full engineering review. Here, a false negative (skips review on a detail that actually needed one) is the dangerous direction — the opposite asymmetry from today's Radley Hall example.
steps: State which error (false positive or false negative) is dangerous here, and why — in one sentence.
Given that asymmetry, would you move the threshold UP or DOWN from 0.5 to catch more true positives?
Name the real-world cost you accept in exchange (more designs sent to review than strictly necessary).
Write the one sentence that would go in this model's model card, stating its chosen threshold and why.
slides.teaching: Correct direction: lower the threshold to prioritize recall in this opposite-risk scenario. Choose the actual value on validation data, then reserve a final test.

slides.title: A probability needs calibration, policy, and uncertainty

steps.label: RELIABILITY
steps.head: Check calibration
steps.body: Compare predicted probabilities with observed frequencies using a reliability diagram.

steps.label: POLICY
steps.head: Freeze a threshold
steps.body: Select the cutoff on validation evidence with a predeclared cost or rate constraint.

steps.label: UNCERTAINTY
steps.head: Quantify a set or interval
steps.body: Conformal methods can wrap a frozen model with coverage-oriented prediction sets under stated assumptions.

steps.label: REFUSE
steps.head: Abstain outside support
steps.body: Escalate unfamiliar, high-impact, or weakly supported cases to measurement or expert review.

slides.teaching: Optional horizon slide. Calibration, discrimination, threshold policy, and uncertainty answer different questions. None authorizes threshold selection on the final test set.

slides.title: Four familiar numbers are not interchangeable
columns: what it cannot support by itself
rows: future performance in a shifted population
conditional certainty for every subgroup or shifted case
slides.callout: Use an untouched final test once; then monitor calibration, drift, subgroup behavior, and the cost of errors after deployment.
slides.teaching: Have pairs diagnose one overclaim in the right column. Explicitly connect the RMSE row to Week 15: plus/minus RMSE is not a prediction interval.

slides.title: A threshold is a stated decision, not a default
takeaways: A confusion matrix's four cells (TN, FP, FN, TP) each carry a different real-world consequence — read them as decisions, not counts.
Choose a threshold on validation data with a predeclared consequence rule; the selected value may happen to equal 0.5.
Freeze model and threshold before opening the final test once; do not retune after seeing its outcomes.
A model card states scope, training ranges, chosen threshold, and honest cross-validated performance — every fitted model should ship with one.
slides.teaching: Close by naming Meeting B's fork explicitly: Track A builds this exact classifier on their own framing; Track B instead deepens Week 13's regression — but both write a model card using tonight's vocabulary.
